stops.name: The Falernian fields, the oxen with fire on their horns
stops.campa: Fabius the Delayer will not fight; he hangs on the hills like weather and lets Italy do the bleeding. When Hannibal gluts the army on the Falernian plain, Fabius quietly locks the one pass out of it. At night Hannibal has fagots lashed to the horns of two thousand captured oxen and the herds driven up the ridges, lit. The pass-guards see an army of torches flowing along the heights, abandon the defile, and fight smoke and cattle in the dark; the real army walks out through the empty pass, plunder and all. Fabius, fearing night and trickery equally, keeps his men in camp and watches the impossible fires burn.

stops.name: Gerunium, the granary winter and the cloud on the mountains
stops.campa: He takes Gerunium with its granaries full and winters in a town used as a barn. Rome, impatient with delay, splits the command: Minucius the bold is raised equal to Fabius the slow, and Hannibal, delighted, the canon says, to have half his enemy foolish, feeds Minucius a small victory, then draws him onto ground stitched with five hundred hidden horse and five thousand foot. The ambush closes; the master of horse is dying in the open when Fabius brings his legions down like a wall and Hannibal, unwilling to buy the whole meal at that price, withdraws. Walking back he says the storm has broken at last.
stops.quote: That cloud that has long been sitting on the tops of the mountains has burst at last in rain and storm.
stops.quote_source: Livy 22.30; Plutarch, Fabius 12, Hannibal on Fabius after the rescue of Minucius

stops.name: Cannae, the second of August
stops.campa: On the plain of the Aufidius, eight legions, the largest army Rome has ever fielded, advance into a line bent forward like a drawn bow: Gauls and Spaniards at the bulge, African veterans at the tips. The bow bends backward as it is pushed; the Romans wedge into their own funeral; the Africans fold onto the flanks; Hasdrubal's horse closes the rear. The double envelopment shuts like a hand. Volturnus drives dust into fifty thousand dying faces; the consul Paullus refuses a horse and dies with his army. It is the ancient world's bloodiest single day, designed by the man who at dawn made his officers laugh.
stops.quote: One thing, Gisgo, is more astonishing than their numbers: in all that great host over there, there is not one man named Gisgo.
stops.quote_source: Plutarch, Fabius 15, to the officer Gisgo, awed by the Roman numbers, at dawn before Cannae

stops.name: The field of Cannae, next dawn: Maharbal's rebuke and the rings
stops.campa: Morning shows what the hand closed on: the dead lying in ranks where the ranks stood, some Romans found with their heads buried in dug earth, having smothered themselves. From the equestrian dead the gold rings are harvested, measured, the tradition says, in bushels, and sent to pour out on the floor of the Carthaginian senate house. Maharbal of the horse begs to ride at once: in five days, he swears, you dine on the Capitol. Hannibal answers that he must have time to deliberate. Then Maharbal says the sentence that the canon has never stopped repeating, and that day's delay, men will say forever, saves Rome.
stops.quote: You know how to win a victory, Hannibal; you do not know how to use one. — And Hannibal: I commend your zeal, Maharbal, but I need time to weigh the plan.
stops.quote_source: Livy 22.51, Vincere scis, Hannibal; victoria uti nescis

stops.name: Capua, the soft winter
stops.campa: Capua, second city of Italy, opens her gates and her houses, and the army that slept in Alpine snow winters in feather beds. Baths, wine, perfume, sleep past dawn: the canon insists that the city accomplished what Cannae could not, and the Romans will say ever after that Capua was Hannibal's Cannae. The register records the tradition and notes what the tradition forgets: that this same softened army will fight undefeated in Italy for thirteen more years. But something does end at Capua: the war stops being a lightning bolt and becomes a long weather.

stops.name: Nola, the wall of Marcellus
stops.campa: Three times he comes at Nola and three times Marcellus, the man Rome calls her sword, as Fabius is her shield, throws him back from the gates, once sallying into the Carthaginian line as it deploys. The repulses are small; their meaning is not. For the first time since the Trebia, Roman soldiers learn that Hannibal's army can be made to step backward. The canon marks Nola the way a physician marks the hour a fever breaks: not the cure, but the first cool morning.

stops.name: Tarentum, the city taken through the hunting gate
stops.campa: Philemenus of Tarentum loves boar-hunting, and the Roman gate-guards have grown used to his horn in the small hours and the game he shares. On the chosen night the horn sounds as always; the postern opens for the hunter, and Hannibal's Africans come through it behind a dead boar carried like a trophy. Ten thousand men enter a sleeping city on the habits of one sentry. The citadel on its spit of rock holds out, Roman and stubborn, commanding the harbor mouth; Hannibal hauls the Tarentine ships across the city streets on wagons and launches them outside the trap: a fleet portaged through a town.

stops.name: The walls of Rome, Hannibal ad portas
stops.campa: To pry the besiegers off Capua he marches on Rome itself, and the cry that will frighten Roman children for five centuries is heard in earnest: Hannibal ad portas. He camps on the Anio, rides two thousand horse under the Colline Gate, examining the walls like a buyer, and hurls a spear over them, the oath's iron touching Rome at last. Twice the armies form for battle; twice hailstorms break the sky and part them. Word comes that the ground under his camp has sold at auction, at full price; he laughs, auctions the Forum's bankers' shops in reply, and turns away. He never sees the walls again.

stops.name: The hill near Venusia, the death of Marcellus
stops.campa: Marcellus, five times consul, the sword of Rome, rides out with a small party to scout a wooded hill between the camps. Numidians are lying in the trees. The sword of Rome dies in a skirmish no poet would have written for him. Hannibal comes to the body and stands over the man who beat him at Nola, takes the signet ring for war's uses, but will not take the corpse: he shrouds it, burns it with honor, and sends the ashes to the son in a silver urn. Even the canon of his enemies keeps this: no Roman ever mourned Marcellus more correctly than Hannibal did.

stops.name: Canusium, the head of Hasdrubal
stops.campa: Hasdrubal has done it: crossed the same Alps in half the time and marches down Italy to join hands with him. The letter naming the meeting-place is taken on the road, and the consul Nero force-marches north in secret, joins his colleague, and destroys Hasdrubal on the Metaurus. Hannibal, waiting in Apulia for word, receives it: Nero's horsemen fling a head before the Carthaginian outposts. Hannibal has it brought to him and looks a long time at the face of the brother who swore no oath and kept his anyway. Then he says the sentence, and draws the army back into Bruttium, into the toe of Italy.
stops.quote: Now I recognize the fortune of Carthage.
stops.quote_source: Livy 27.51, agnoscere se fortunam Carthaginis, on seeing Hasdrubal's head

stops.name: Cape Lacinium, the bronze tablet in Hera's temple
stops.campa: At the temple of Hera Lacinia, Hannibal dedicates an altar and a great bronze tablet engraved in Punic and Greek: his own account of his marches and musters, set down in the goddess's keeping. Polybius will stand here, copy the figures, and trust bronze over rumor. The temple holds a column of solid gold; the tradition says Hannibal bored it to test it and meant to take it, and the goddess warned him in a dream that she would take his one good eye, so he left the column and crowned it with a golden heifer cast from the borings. Even the wonders obey him only halfway.

stops.name: Croton, the recall to Africa
stops.campa: Scipio is in Africa, and the senate of Carthage sends the order no Roman army could compel: come home. Fifteen years in Italy, undefeated in the field, and it ends with an instruction on a ship. The canon says he gnashed his teeth and could scarcely keep from tears; that he raged at the men, not Rome, who starved him of reinforcement; that he cursed himself for not marching on Rome with his sword bloody. The grim tradition adds that Italian soldiers refusing the crossing were killed in the goddess's precinct. He looks back at Italy as few exiles ever looked back at their own country. Then Africa.
